title: Sources: social media limits and well-being
stem: Source A (fictional data): 120 university students were randomly allocated to limit social media to 30 minutes a day or to use it as usual for four weeks. Loneliness was measured on a 20–80 scale before and after. Source B (fictional): semi-structured interviews with 8 students from the limited group. Common themes were "missing out on plans", "more time to sleep" and "feeling calmer after the first week". One interviewer conducted and coded all the interviews.

data.caption: Source A: mean loneliness scores (higher = lonelier)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Interpret the results shown in Source A.
markscheme: both groups started at similar levels (46 vs 45)
loneliness fell by 6 points in the limited group but only 1 point in the usual-use group
this suggests limiting social media reduced loneliness, though significance is not reported

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Analyse the extent to which Source A supports a causal conclusion.
markscheme: random allocation controls participant variables, supporting a causal claim
a control group allows comparison with change over time
self-report loneliness scale may be affected by demand characteristics as participants knew their condition
compliance with the limit is not verified / may rely on self-report
no measure of spread or significance test given
sample of university students limits generalization; conclusion stated

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discuss the credibility of Source B.
markscheme: credibility = how far findings reflect participants' experiences
one researcher conducting and coding interviews risks researcher bias
no researcher triangulation or member checking reported
small sample from one group limits transferability
strength: semi-structured interviews give rich data explaining how changes were experienced
suggest improvements, e.g. second coder, reflexivity statement, member checking

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using both sources and your own knowledge, evaluate the role of technology in well-being.
markscheme: uses Source A: experimental evidence that reducing use lowers loneliness
uses Source B: themes suggest mechanisms (more sleep, calmer) but also costs (missing out)
sources combined: quantitative effect explained by qualitative experience
own knowledge: Hunt et al. (2018) similar findings with a 10-minute-per-platform limit
own knowledge: Przybylski & Weinstein (2017) Goldilocks hypothesis, moderate use not harmful
causality/bidirectionality: most research is correlational; low well-being may increase use
measurement issues: self-reported screen time and well-being
consideration of individual or cultural differences in how technology is used
balanced, justified conclusion on the role of technology
parts.notes: In the real Paper 3 the synthesis question is worth 15 marks and needs at least three sources; it is shortened here.
